title: Non-deterministic finite-state automata
text:
A non-deterministic finite-state automaton loosens some of the restrictions imposed by a DFA; chiefly, by allowing the transitions between states to be characterized by a relation, rather than by a function. Partee et al. (1990), Definition 17.6 (p. 462), presents them as follows.
As non-deterministic finite-state automaton (NFA) is a quintuple \(⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩\), where:
Instead of a function \(δ\), we have a relation \(Δ\) which associates pairs of states from \(K\) and strings over the alphabet with new states from \(K\). It is because \(Δ\) can associate any given pair of input state and string with potentially more than one output state that we say NFAs are non-deterministic.
Note also that this definition of NFAs allows not only words—but strings—to be associated with the transition from one state to the next.

title: Relations
text:
If we have a collection of sets \(A_{1}\) through \(A_{n}\), then we can take an \(n\)-ary relation on those sets. An \(n\)-ary relation on the sets \(A_{1}, ..., A_{n}\) is a set \(R\) such that \(R ⊆ A_{1} × ... × A_{n}\). In the special case of a binary relation on two sets \(A\) and \(B\), \(R\) is a set of pairs \(⟨a, b⟩\), such that \(a ∈ A\) and \(b ∈ B\). That is, \(R ⊆ A × B\). For \(n\)-ary relations \(R\), if the \(n\)-tuple \(⟨a₁, ..., aₙ⟩\) is a member of \(R\), we can indicate this by writing \[R(a₁, ..., aₙ)\]
An important operation on relations is relation composition. Given a relation \(R_{1} ⊂ A × B\) and a relation \(R_{2} ⊆ B × C\), their composition \[R_{2} ∘ R_{1}\] which is a subset of \(A × C\), is defined as \[R_{2} ∘ R_{1} = \{⟨x, y⟩ ∣ \text{there is some $z$ such that } ⟨x, z⟩ ∈ R_{1} \text{ and } ⟨z, y⟩ ∈ R_{2}\}\] That is, \(R_{2} ∘ R_{1}\) is gotten by relating an element of \(A\) to an element of \(C\) just in case there is some element of \(B\) related to the first element by \(R_{1}\) and to the second element by \(R_{2}\).
If \(R\) is a relation on \(A\), then we will write \(R^{n}\) to refer to the result of composing \(R\) with itself \(n\) times. By convention: \[\begin{align*}
R^{0} &= \{⟨x, x⟩ ∣ x ∈ A\}\\
R^{} &= R\\
Rⁿ &= R^{n - 1} ∘ R
\end{align*}\] If \(R ⊆ A × B\), we may define its inverse as the relation \(R^{-1} ⊆ B × A\) such that \(⟨y, x⟩ ∈ R^{-1}\) just in case \(⟨x, y⟩ ∈ R\). That is, \(R^{-1}\) is just like \(R\), but “flipped around”.

title: Languages
text:
We write ‘\(A^{n}\)’ to refer to the result of taking the product of the set \(A\) with itself \(n\) times. As a matter of convention, we will adopt the following equivalences. \[\begin{align*}
A^0 &=_{def} \{ϵ\} \tag{$ϵ$ is the empty string} \\
A^1 &=_{def} A \\
A^n &=_{def} A^{n-1} × A
\end{align*}\] To define a language, we first define a set \(Σ\), which we call the alphabet, words, or lexicon of the language. These can be anything, in principle (phonetic forms, sets of syntactic features, blades of grass, etc.). Then, a language over the alphabet \(Σ\) is some set \(L\) such that \[L ⊆ Σ^{*}\] where \[Σ^{*} ≝ ⋃_{i ∈ ℕ} Σ^{i}\] Thus \(L\) is a set of \(n\)-tuples of words from \(Σ\) of any length \(n\). When we talk about languages, we will refer to tuples as strings and adopt the convention of writing, e.g., the string ⟨ the, dog, is, friendly ⟩ simply as the dog is friendly.

title: Examples
text:
Here are some examples of proofs of some basic facts about sets.

First example
Show that \(A ⊆ A ∪ B\).
The definition of subset says that this holds if everything in \(A\) is also in \(A ∪ B\). The definition of union says that any \(x ∈ A ∪ B\) if \(x ∈ A\) or \(x ∈ B\). Thus any \(x ∈ A\) is such that \(x ∈ A ∪ B\), as needed.


Second example
Let \(A, B ⊆ C\), and let’s introduce the notation ‘\(¬X\)’ for \(C - X\).
Show that \(¬(A ∪ B) ⊆ ¬A ∩ ¬B\).
Assume \(x ∈ ¬(A ∪ B)\) (for arbitrary \(x\)); then, our goal is show that \(x\) must be in \(¬A ∩ ¬B\). By definition, \(x ∈ C\), but \(x ∉ A ∪ B\). Hence, \(x ∉ A\) (or else, we would have that \(x ∈ A ∪ B\)). But because, by hypothesis, \(x ∈ C\), we now have that \(x ∈ ¬A\). A similar argument applies to \(¬B\)! Thus \(x ∈ ¬A ∩ ¬B\). Since \(x\) is arbitrary, the argument extends to any element of \(¬(A ∪ B)\), as needed to show that the two sets are in a subset relation.

title: Syllabus
text:
Bird’s-eye view
The goal of this course is to acquaint you with the study of formal linguistic complexity. Specifically, we will cover complexity classes of languages, focusing on regular, context-free, context-sensitive, recursive, and recursively enumerable languages. We’ll explore each class of languages in terms of: (a) the formal grammars that generate languages in that class; and (b) the abstract machines that recognize languages in the class. Along the way, we’ll discuss hypotheses about the complexity of natural language (e.g., the subregular hypothesis in phonology, and the hypothesis that natural language syntax is mildly context-sensitive), as well as some grammar formalisms which have been proposed to capture these hypotheses.

title: Functions
text:
A function from a set \(A\) to a set \(B\) is a map from elements of \(A\) to elements of \(B\) which pairs each element of \(A\) with exactly one element of \(B\). If \(f\) is such a function, we write \[f : A → B\] to indicate this. We call \(A\) the domain of the function, and we call \(B\) the codomain of the function. If \(a ∈ A\), then we write \[f(a)\] to pick out the unique \(b ∈ B\) that \(f\) pairs \(a\) up with. In case \(f(a) = b\) (for some \(a\) and \(b\)), we call \(a\) the argument of the function \(f\), and we call \(b\) the value of the function \(f\) on \(a\).
Kind of like with relations, the definition of (unary) functions can be generalized to that for n-ary functions by considering the latter to be a map from the product of \(n\) sets \(A₁, ..., Aₙ\) to a set \(B\). If \(f\) is such an \(n\)-ary function, we write \[f : A_1 × ... × A_n → B\] to indicate this. Given \(n\) arguments \(a₁ ∈ A₁, ..., aₙ ∈ Aₙ\), we write \[f(a_1, ..., a_n)\] to pick out out the \(b ∈ B\) that \(f\) maps \(a₁, ..., aₙ\) to.1
Two properties of functions are sometimes important for certain purposes: if a function \(f\) from \(A\) (or \(A₁, ..., Aₙ\)) to \(B\) pairs each element \(a ∈ A\) (or (n)-tuple \(a₁ ∈ A₁, ..., aₙ ∈ Aₙ\)) with a different element \(b ∈ B\), we call \(f\) an injection (or a one-to-one function). If for each \(b ∈ B\), \(f\) pairs some or other \(a ∈ A\) (or \(n\)-tuple \(a₁, ..., aₙ\)) with it, we call \(f\) a surjection (or an onto function). If \(f\) is both an injection and a surjection, we call it a bijection from \(A\) (or \(A₁, ..., Aₙ\)) to \(B\).
Importantly, there is a corresponding notion of function composition. We need only consider functions from \(A\) to \(B\) a type of relation on \(A\) and \(B\)—one that relations every element in \(A\) to exactly one element in \(B\). Given functions \(f : A → B\) and \(g : B → C\), their composition \[g ∘ f : A → C\] is such that \((g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))\), for any \(x ∈ A\). In the same vein, if \[f : A → A\] then we may write ‘\(f^{n}\)’ to denote the function which “applies \(f\) to an element of \(A\) \(n\) times”. For example, \(f^{3}(a) = f(f(f(a)))\).

title: Functions
text:
Footnotes


 Note that a function \(f : A → B\) can be considered to be a relation on \(A\) and \(B\) where, for each \(a ∈ A\), there is exactly one \(b ∈ B\) such that \(⟨a, b⟩ ∈ f\). More generally, an \(n\)-ary function can be considered an \((n+1)\)-ary relation. This is just a particular way of encoding functions as relations—it isn’t the definition of a function, i.e., a map between sets, as above.↩︎

title: Products
text:
Given two sets \(A\) and \(B\), we take their binary Cartesian product \[(A × B)\] to be the set of pairs of elements \(⟨a, b⟩\), where \(a ∈ A\) and \(b ∈ B\). We call \(a\) the first component (or projection) of such a pair and \(b\) the second component. Given a pair \(p\), we will sometimes write ‘\(p_{1}\)’ to refer to its first component and ‘\(p_{2}\)’ to refer to its second component. In particular: \[⟨x, y⟩_{1} = x\] \[⟨x, y⟩_{2} = y\]
The following statement is also true: \[⟨x_{1}, x_{2}⟩ = x\] That is, if you take the first and second components of a pair and then pair them back up, you haven’t created anything new!
We can generalize binary products to \(n\)-ary products by considering the former to correspond to the special case where \(n = 2\). For the general case \[A₁ × ... × A_{n-1} × Aₙ\] we can encode this product as \[(...(A₁ × ... × A_{n-1}) × Aₙ)\] For example, \(A × B × C\) is just \(((A × B) × C)\); its members are, therefore, pairs \(⟨⟨a, b⟩, c⟩\), which is just how we can encode 3-tuples \(⟨a, b, c⟩\).

title: Sets
text:
A set is, intuitively speaking, a collection of objects, which we call the elements or members of the set. Any talk about sets is understood in the context of some universe of discourse. All sets inhabit this universe, as do any of the objects which we may consider to be members of a set. We may, for example, want to have things like words or natural numbers inhabit this universe. When analyzing languages, we may want to include other things too, like the words of some alphabet.
For any set \(A\) and any object \(a\) in the universe, either one of the following two things is true. \[\begin{align*}
a ∈ A \tag{$a$ is a member of $A$}\\
a ∉ A \tag{$a$ is not a member of $A$}
\end{align*}\] Crucially, sets are defined by their members. That means that, for every \(a\) in the universe, if \(a ∈ A\) if and only if \(a ∈ B\), then \(A\) and \(B\) are the same set. This is the principle of extensionality for sets.
We will generally help ourselves to two kinds of notation for specifying sets: list notation and predicate (or “set-comprehension”, or “set-builder”) notation. In list notation, we define a set by enumerating its elements between curly braces. For example, \[\{1, 2, 3, George Washington\}\] is just the set \(A\) such that \(1 ∈ A\), \(2 ∈ A\), \(3 ∈ A\), and nothing else is \(∈ A\). Because of extensionality, \(\{1, 2, 3, GW\}\) is the same set as \(\{1, 1, 2, 3, GW\}\) is the same set as \(\{3, GW, 2, 2, 1\}\), etc. Using predicate notation, we can specify the very same set as \[\{x ∣ x = 1 \text{ or } x = 2 \text{ or } x = 3 \text{ or } x = GW\}\] In general, in writing ‘\(\{a\) \(|\) \(φ\}\)’, \(a\) will be an expression with some number of variables occurring in it (things like \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and so on), and \(φ\) will be a sentence expressing a condition on the values of these variables. Any number of the variables in \(a\), and generally only these, can occur in \(φ\). In the example above, \(a\) just was the variable \(x\), and the condition expressed was that the value of \(x\) be either 1, 2, 3, or George.
But we could also use predicate notation, as in \[\{x + 1 ∣ x = 1 \text{ or } x = 2 \text{ or } x = 3\}\] where \(a\) is the complex expression ‘\(x +
1\)’, to specify the set \(\{2, 3, 4\}\).
Importantly, there is an empty set, which we’ll write ‘\(\varnothing\)’. It has no members. As a result, \(a ∉ \varnothing\) for every \(a\) in the universe. The empty set can also be written using list notation, as ‘\(\{\}\)’.

title: The equivalence between DFAs and NFAs
text:
It turns out that DFAs and NFAs are equivalent, in the sense that they characterize the same set of languages—the regular languages. Not only that, but it is possible to convert between them: there is a systematic procedure for turning any random DFA into an NFA, as well as one for turning any NFA into a DFA.
To show this, we first provide the following alternative definition of NFAs, which is equivalent to the definition provided by Partee et al. (1990). According to this definition, \(K\), \(Σ\), \(q_{0}\), and \(F\) remain the same, but we present the transition relation slightly differently. Instead of a relation \[Δ ⊆ (K × Σ^{*}) × K\] we define a function \[Δ : K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}) → 2^{K}\] That is, \(Δ\) is defined instead as a function that takes pairs of (1) states, and (2) either elements of the alphabet or \(ϵ\), onto sets of new states.
Note that any such function is equivalent to a relation on \(K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\})\) and \(K\): given such a function \(Δ\), you can simply define the relation \[R = \{⟨q, x, q′⟩ ∣ q′ ∈ Δ(q, x)\}\] Note that if \(Δ(q, x) = \varnothing\) for some \(q ∈ K\) and \(x ∈ Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}\), then \(q\) and \(x\) aren’t related to any output state by the relation \(R\).
Meanwhile, if you have a relation \(R ⊆ (K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\})) × K\), you can simply define the function \[Δ(q, x) = \{q′ ∈ K ∣ ⟨q, x, q′⟩ ∈ R\}\] Note (correspondingly) that for any \(q ∈ K\) and \(x ∈ Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}\), if \(R\) doesn’t relate \(q\) and \(x\) to any output state, then \(Δ(q, x) = \varnothing\).

title: The equivalence between DFAs and NFAs
text:
Translating DFAs into NFAs
To show that any DFA yields an equivalent NFA, one need only adjust its transition function \(δ\) so that it instead maps pairs of states and words of the alphabet onto sets of output states. Given a word \(w\) and state \(q\), which set of states should the pair \(⟨q, w⟩\) be mapped to? Simply, the one-element set \(\{δ(q, w)\}\), whatever that is.
Thus given a DFA \(⟨K, Σ, δ, q_{0}, F⟩\), we can define the NFA \(⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩\), where \(Δ(q, w) = \{δ(q, w)\}\) and \(Δ(q, ϵ) = \varnothing\) (for any \(q\)). In a sense, every DFA already is an NFA; we are just rearranging the definition slightly.

title: The equivalence between DFAs and NFAs
text:
Translating NFAs into DFAs
Going the other direction is more interesting. To do this, there are a couple of definitions it is useful to provide.

\(ϵ\)-only paths
First, we need the notion of a finite \(ϵ\)-only path. Given some NFA, a finite \(ϵ\)-only path can be viewed as a sequence of transitions (possibly of length 0) through its state diagram which only involve \(ϵ\). In the state diagram above, for instance, there is exactly one finite \(ϵ\)-only path of length at least 1 (every state has a length-0 \(ϵ\)-only path to itself): the one from \(q_{0}\) to \(q_{a}\). The NFA represented by this state diagram has three finite \(ϵ\)-only paths of length at least 1 (again, every state has a length-0 \(ϵ\)-only path to itself): one from \(q_{0}\) to \(q_{a}\); one from \(q_{a}\) to \(q_{b}\); and one from \(q_{0}\) to \(q_{b}\). The last path comes from sequencing the first two paths.
More formally, given the transition function \(Δ : K × (Σ ∪ \{ϵ\}) → 2^{K}\), we can define a relation \(Δ_{ϵ} ⊆ K × K\): \[Δ_{ϵ} ≝ \{⟨q, q′⟩ ∣ q′ ∈ Δ(q, ϵ)\}\] That is, \(Δ_{ϵ}\) relates \(q\) to \(q′\) just in case you can reach \(q′\) from \(q\) in one step by reading an \(ϵ\).
Let us now define the notion of composing \(Δ_{ϵ}\) with itself an arbitrary number of times, denoted \(Δ_{ϵ}^{n}\) (where \(n\) is the relevant “arbitrary” number). \[Δ_{ϵ}^{0} ≝ \{⟨q, q⟩ ∣ q ∈ K\}\] \[Δ_{ϵ}^{n+1} ≝ Δ_{ϵ} ∘ Δ_{ϵ}^{n}\] Thus \(Δ_{ϵ}^{0}\) is the identity relation on \(K\); \(Δ_{ϵ}^{1}\) is just \(Δ_{ϵ}\) itself; \(Δ_{ϵ}^{2}\) is \(Δ_{ϵ} ∘ Δ_{ϵ}\) (i.e., \(Δ_{ϵ}\) composed with itself); and so on. Then the following relation, \(Δ_{ϵ}^{*}\), is known as the reflexive transitive closure of the relation \(Δ_{ϵ}\): \[Δ_{ϵ}^{*} ≝ ⋃_{i ∈ ℕ}Δ_{ϵ}^{i}\] In words, \(Δ_{ϵ}^{*}\) relates two states \(q\) and \(q′\) just in case there is a finite (possibly length-0) \(ϵ\)-only path from \(q\) to \(q′\) in the state diagram of the NFA whose transition function is \(Δ\). Because length-0 paths are also allowed, the relation is reflexive; i.e., it relates any state in \(K\) (the set of states) to itself.


ϵ-closure by finite paths
For any set of states \(Q ⊆ K\), we can define its epsilon closure by finite paths \(Ε(Q)\): \[Ε(Q) ≝ \{q′ ∣ \text{there is some } q \text{ in } Q \text{, and } ⟨q, q′⟩ ∈ Δ_{ϵ}^{*}\}\] In words, given any set \(Q\) of states, \(Ε(Q)\) has as an element every state in \(Q\) itself, as well as every state you can get to from a state in \(Q\) via a finite \(ϵ\)-only path.
Consider again the state diagram given just above, and consider the set \(\{q_{0}\}\). Then, \(Ε(\{q_{0}\}) = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}\}\); this is the set of states reachable from \(q_{0}\) by some finite \(ϵ\)-only path. Note that if we instead consider the set \(\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}\), we get the same set again: \(Ε(\{q_{0}, q_{a}\}) = \{q_{0}, q_{a}, q_{b}\}\).


The translation
We can now straightforwardly define the translation from an arbitrary NFA to its DFA which accepts the same language. Given an NFA \(⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩\), we define the corresponding DFA \(⟨K′, Σ′, δ, q_{0}′, F′⟩\) as follows.

\(K′ = 2^{K}\)
\(Σ′ = Σ\)
\(δ(Q, w) = Ε(⋃_{q ∈ Q}Δ(q, w))\) (where \(w ∈ Σ\))
\(q_{0}′ = Ε(\{q_{0}\})\)
\(F′ = \{Q ∣ Q ∩ F ≠ \varnothing\}\)
